principle: Each project belongs to one system family, has one primary role, and carries orthogonal traits. Scores are comparable only inside the same score profile.

system_families.name: Memory systems
system_families.definition: Systems whose primary value is capturing, organizing, preserving, retrieving, or reasoning over durable knowledge.

system_families.name: Agent systems
system_families.definition: Systems whose primary value is planning and taking actions through tools on a person's behalf.

system_families.name: Assistant systems
system_families.definition: End-user conversational systems whose primary value is helping a person reason, create, research, and optionally act across broad tasks.

primary_roles.name: Human-first PKM / workspace
primary_roles.definition: A user-facing system whose canonical workflow is human writing, organizing, linking, and revisiting knowledge.

primary_roles.name: AI knowledge app / RAG brain
primary_roles.definition: A user-facing assistant that ingests documents or connected sources and answers, searches, summarizes, or automates over them.

primary_roles.name: External agent-memory service
primary_roles.definition: A replaceable library or service that extracts, stores, retrieves, and manages durable memories through an SDK, API, or tool protocol.

primary_roles.name: Temporal context / knowledge-graph engine
primary_roles.definition: Infrastructure that represents entities, relationships, provenance, and changing truth over time.

primary_roles.name: Human–agent memory bridge
primary_roles.definition: A compatibility layer that exposes human-owned files or workspaces to multiple agents.

primary_roles.name: Ambient capture / lifelogging
primary_roles.definition: A passive collector that records digital activity without requiring deliberate note creation.

primary_roles.name: Retrieval / storage infrastructure
primary_roles.definition: A low-level vector, graph, lexical, or multimodal store used to build memory systems.

primary_roles.name: General work agent
primary_roles.definition: An end-user agent that accepts broad delegated outcomes and executes multi-step knowledge work across files, the web, applications, and scheduled workflows.

primary_roles.name: Coding agent
primary_roles.definition: An interactive agent that reads, edits, runs, and reasons about software projects.

primary_roles.name: Research agent
primary_roles.definition: An agent that plans multi-step information gathering and synthesizes cited findings.

primary_roles.name: Browser / computer-use agent
primary_roles.definition: An agent specialized in operating browsers, desktops, or other graphical interfaces.

primary_roles.name: Data-analysis / text-to-SQL agent
primary_roles.definition: An agent that plans, executes, validates, and explains structured-data queries or analyses through database and analytics tools.

primary_roles.name: Stateful agent runtime / harness
primary_roles.definition: A persistent agent runtime that owns identity, durable state, skills, schedules, and memory lifecycle.

primary_roles.name: Coding-agent workflow / skill stack
primary_roles.definition: Prompts, roles, tools, and process that turn coding agents into a repeatable software-delivery system.

primary_roles.name: Multi-agent orchestrator
primary_roles.definition: A system for coordinating specialized agents, handoffs, workflows, and shared execution.

primary_roles.name: Agent framework / SDK
primary_roles.definition: A developer framework or builder for creating tool-using, controllable, observable agent applications.

primary_roles.name: General AI assistant
primary_roles.definition: A provider-branded conversational product spanning information, creation, files, research, personalization, and optional actions.

primary_roles.name: Enterprise work assistant
primary_roles.definition: A tenant or workspace assistant grounded in organizational systems with connectors, governance, administration, or business actions.

primary_roles.name: Multi-model chat client
primary_roles.definition: An end-user product whose primary value is presenting or routing multiple interchangeable model backends through a persistent chat workspace.

provider_relationships.name: Provider-native
provider_relationships.definition: The primary supported path is officially coupled to one model-provider ecosystem.

provider_relationships.name: Multi-provider
provider_relationships.definition: The project maintains first-class integrations with multiple named model backends.

provider_relationships.name: Provider-agnostic
provider_relationships.definition: The project exposes a substitutable backend contract rather than making one provider the primary path.

inference_service_types.name: Direct model API
inference_service_types.definition: A model developer operates the primary API for its own model families.

inference_service_types.name: Cloud model platform
inference_service_types.definition: A governed cloud platform serves models from multiple publishers alongside cloud-native deployment controls.

inference_service_types.name: Managed inference host
inference_service_types.definition: An infrastructure operator serves selected third-party or open-weight models through a managed API.

inference_service_types.name: Routing aggregator
inference_service_types.definition: A unified API selects among upstream models or inference operators using routing and fallback policy.

inference_delivery_modes.name: On-demand
inference_delivery_modes.definition: Shared managed capacity is billed or limited by request or token use.

inference_delivery_modes.name: Batch
inference_delivery_modes.definition: Asynchronous jobs trade immediate response for separate capacity or pricing.

inference_delivery_modes.name: Reserved capacity
inference_delivery_modes.definition: Customers purchase or reserve a defined throughput tier or capacity allocation.

inference_delivery_modes.name: Dedicated endpoint
inference_delivery_modes.definition: A customer-controlled deployment receives isolated serving resources or an endpoint.

inference_model_sources.name: First-party models
inference_model_sources.definition: Models developed by the service operator.

inference_model_sources.name: Third-party proprietary models
inference_model_sources.definition: Closed model families supplied by another publisher.

inference_model_sources.name: Open-weight models
inference_model_sources.definition: Externally published model weights served by the operator; weight terms remain model-specific.

inference_model_sources.name: Customer-supplied models
inference_model_sources.definition: Customers can import or deploy their own eligible model artifacts or weights.

inference_api_styles.name: OpenAI-compatible
inference_api_styles.definition: A service implements a documented subset or adaptation of OpenAI API conventions.

inference_api_styles.name: Anthropic API
inference_api_styles.definition: Anthropic's first-party Messages and related API contracts.

inference_api_styles.name: Anthropic-compatible
inference_api_styles.definition: A service implements a documented subset or adaptation of Anthropic API conventions.

inference_api_styles.name: AWS-native
inference_api_styles.definition: Amazon Bedrock APIs and AWS SDK contracts.

inference_api_styles.name: Google Cloud-native
inference_api_styles.definition: Vertex AI REST, RPC, and Google Cloud SDK contracts.

inference_api_styles.name: Service-native
inference_api_styles.definition: A service-specific REST, RPC, or SDK contract not represented by another named API style.

local_runtime_types.name: Desktop runner
local_runtime_types.definition: A packaged application or command-line product that installs on a personal machine and manages model download, storage, and local serving as one product.

local_runtime_types.name: Server engine
local_runtime_types.definition: An inference server built for sustained multi-request serving, batching, and deployment onto operator-controlled hardware.

local_runtime_types.name: Embedded library
local_runtime_types.definition: An inference implementation consumed as a library or binary that host applications embed rather than operate as a standing service.

local_runtime_types.name: Compatibility gateway
local_runtime_types.definition: A self-hosted server that presents a compatible API surface over one or more local inference backends.

runtime_accelerators.name: CPU
runtime_accelerators.definition: Documented execution on general-purpose processors without a dedicated accelerator.

runtime_accelerators.name: NVIDIA CUDA
runtime_accelerators.definition: Documented execution on NVIDIA GPUs through the CUDA toolchain.

runtime_accelerators.name: AMD ROCm
runtime_accelerators.definition: Documented execution on AMD GPUs through the ROCm toolchain.

runtime_accelerators.name: Apple Metal
runtime_accelerators.definition: Documented execution on Apple silicon GPUs through Metal.

runtime_accelerators.name: Vulkan
runtime_accelerators.definition: Documented execution through the cross-vendor Vulkan compute backend.

runtime_accelerators.name: SYCL
runtime_accelerators.definition: Documented execution through SYCL, covering Intel GPU targets.

runtime_accelerators.name: OpenCL
runtime_accelerators.definition: Documented execution through the OpenCL compute API, covering Adreno, Mali, and other cross-vendor GPU targets.

runtime_accelerators.name: WebGPU
runtime_accelerators.definition: Documented execution through the WebGPU browser compute API, covering in-page and cross-platform GPU targets.

runtime_accelerators.name: NPU
runtime_accelerators.definition: Documented execution on a dedicated neural processing unit, such as those integrated into recent client processors.

runtime_accelerators.name: DirectML
runtime_accelerators.definition: Documented execution through Microsoft's DirectML backend, covering vendor-neutral GPU acceleration on Windows.

runtime_accelerators.name: Multi-GPU
runtime_accelerators.definition: Documented execution across more than one accelerator on a single host or across hosts.

runtime_model_formats.name: GGUF
runtime_model_formats.definition: The quantized single-file weight format used by the llama.cpp family of runtimes.

runtime_model_formats.name: Safetensors
runtime_model_formats.definition: The safe tensor serialization format used by mainstream transformer checkpoints.

runtime_model_formats.name: PyTorch checkpoints
runtime_model_formats.definition: Native PyTorch weight checkpoints loaded through the framework's own serialization.

runtime_model_formats.name: MLX
runtime_model_formats.definition: Weights prepared for Apple's MLX array framework on Apple silicon.

runtime_model_formats.name: GPTQ
runtime_model_formats.definition: Post-training quantized checkpoints produced by the GPTQ method.

runtime_model_formats.name: FP8
runtime_model_formats.definition: Eight-bit floating point weights or activations on accelerators that support them.

runtime_model_formats.name: TensorFlow SavedModel
runtime_model_formats.definition: TensorFlow's SavedModel graph directory, the versioned artifact produced by exporting a trained TensorFlow model.

runtime_model_formats.name: MLC compiled
runtime_model_formats.definition: Weights and model libraries produced by MLC LLM's compilation pipeline for a specific target.

runtime_model_formats.name: ONNX
runtime_model_formats.definition: Models exported to the Open Neural Network Exchange graph format, optionally with quantized weights.

runtime_serving_modes.name: Single stream
runtime_serving_modes.definition: One request served at a time, sufficient for interactive personal use.

runtime_serving_modes.name: Continuous batching
runtime_serving_modes.definition: Requests joined into and retired from in-flight batches to sustain accelerator utilization.

runtime_serving_modes.name: Parallel requests
runtime_serving_modes.definition: Concurrent request handling through configured workers, slots, or sequences.

runtime_serving_modes.name: Distributed serving
runtime_serving_modes.definition: Model or request distribution across multiple accelerators or hosts through parallelism strategies.

runtime_serving_modes.name: Speculative decoding
runtime_serving_modes.definition: Draft-and-verify decoding that trades additional computation for reduced generation latency.

runtime_deployment_surfaces.name: Desktop application
runtime_deployment_surfaces.definition: A graphical application installed on a personal operating system.

runtime_deployment_surfaces.name: Local CLI
runtime_deployment_surfaces.definition: A command-line executable operated on the user's own machine.

runtime_deployment_surfaces.name: Library
runtime_deployment_surfaces.definition: An importable package or linkable binary embedded in a host application.

runtime_deployment_surfaces.name: Container
runtime_deployment_surfaces.definition: A published container image intended for containerized execution.

runtime_deployment_surfaces.name: Orchestrated cluster
runtime_deployment_surfaces.definition: Documented deployment onto an orchestrator such as Kubernetes with scaling guidance.

runtime_deployment_surfaces.name: Mobile or embedded device
runtime_deployment_surfaces.definition: Documented deployment onto phones, tablets, or embedded hardware rather than a personal computer or server.

runtime_deployment_surfaces.name: Browser
runtime_deployment_surfaces.definition: Documented execution inside a web browser page without a separate local server process.

dimensions.definition: Documented production controls, lifecycle stability, administration, support, and readiness for sustained service use; it does not infer unreported uptime or throughput.
Documented retention, training-use, deletion, isolation, tenant, and privacy controls across the represented service boundary.
Customer control over processing geography, network boundaries, regional endpoints, and isolated or dedicated placement.
Documented on-demand, batch, reserved, dedicated, and scaling paths for materially different workload shapes.
Portability and integration quality across documented APIs, compatibility contracts, SDK conventions, and deployment interfaces.
Documented traffic steering, fallback, multi-region capacity, replica, priority, or recovery controls without treating raw latency as stable.
Fine-tuning, customer models, version control, deployment configuration, and lifecycle management for supported model artifacts.
Clarity and specificity of authoritative documentation for terms, data handling, regions, limits, availability, and operational exceptions.
Documented and supported CPU, CUDA, ROCm, Metal, Vulkan, and multi-accelerator execution paths for the reviewed runtime itself.
Breadth of supported weight formats, quantization schemes, and model architectures the runtime can load and execute.
Documented batching, parallel request handling, cache management, and distributed serving capability; it does not measure throughput or latency.
Documented native and compatible endpoints, embeddings, tool calling, and structured output, and their portability across clients.
Install paths, container images, orchestration guidance, resource limits, authentication, and upgrade practice.
Fetching, pinning, custom model import, adapter support, storage control, and removal for local model artifacts.
Metrics, health endpoints, logging, request introspection, and administrative surfaces for an operator running the software.
Clarity and specificity of authoritative documentation for accelerators, formats, serving, deployment, limits, and known exceptions.

specification_types.name: Protocol
specification_types.definition: A machine-readable contract for exchanging messages, capabilities, context, or events between independently implemented components.

specification_types.name: Metadata schema
specification_types.definition: A versioned machine-readable vocabulary for describing identity, capabilities, domains, locators, or other discoverable metadata.

specification_types.name: Instruction convention
specification_types.definition: A file-naming and discovery convention that gives agents repository or project guidance without defining a wire protocol.

specification_types.name: Capability format
specification_types.definition: A portable package format for instructions, metadata, scripts, and resources that teach an agent a reusable capability.

specification_types.name: Package format
specification_types.definition: A distributable bundle contract that composes capabilities, commands, agents, hooks, or integrations.

specification_scopes.name: Tool and data integration
specification_scopes.definition: Connects model applications to tools, resources, prompts, and external data.

specification_scopes.name: Web and agent integration
specification_scopes.definition: Lets web pages expose structured, user-mediated capabilities to browser or embedded agents.

specification_scopes.name: Agent-to-agent interaction
specification_scopes.definition: Supports discovery, task delegation, messages, artifacts, and lifecycle between independent agents.

specification_scopes.name: Agent identity and discovery
specification_scopes.definition: Describes agent identity, capabilities, endpoints, and discovery metadata across independently operated systems.

specification_scopes.name: Agent–user interaction
specification_scopes.definition: Streams agent state, events, actions, and human input between a runtime and user-facing application.

specification_scopes.name: Agent–client integration
specification_scopes.definition: Connects coding agents to editors, IDEs, and other interactive clients.

specification_scopes.name: Project instructions
specification_scopes.definition: Supplies persistent repository or workspace guidance to compatible coding agents.

specification_scopes.name: Capability packaging
specification_scopes.definition: Packages focused, reusable agent capabilities with progressive context loading.

specification_scopes.name: Plugin packaging
specification_scopes.definition: Bundles multiple agent extensions behind one installable manifest and directory layout.

specification_scopes.name: Agent transactions
specification_scopes.definition: Coordinates commerce, authorization, checkout, payment, receipt, or order evidence between users, agents, merchants, and payment parties.

specification_statuses.name: Published
specification_statuses.definition: A named release or stable published specification is available.

specification_statuses.name: Evolving
specification_statuses.definition: The artifact is public and implementable, but its current contract is rolling or actively changing.

specification_statuses.name: Vendor-specific
specification_statuses.definition: A documented convention owned by one product ecosystem rather than an independent open standard.

specification_statuses.name: Superseded
specification_statuses.definition: The artifact remains useful historically but a successor is the recommended integration path.

architectures.name: Vector / embedding index
architectures.note: An architecture trait, not a product category.

architectures.name: Undisclosed service-managed internals
architectures.note: Use when authoritative product evidence establishes a managed system but does not establish its storage architecture.

deployment_modes.name: Desktop application
deployment_modes.definition: A desktop application the user installs and runs.

deployment_modes.name: Mobile application
deployment_modes.definition: A mobile application the user installs and runs.

deployment_modes.name: Local CLI
deployment_modes.definition: A command-line program the user runs on their own machine.

deployment_modes.name: IDE extension
deployment_modes.definition: An extension that runs inside an editor or IDE.

deployment_modes.name: Embedded library
deployment_modes.definition: A package the user embeds in an application they build, including helpers that application calls to serve its own endpoints.

deployment_modes.name: Self-hosted service
deployment_modes.definition: A service the project itself ships, which the user deploys and operates on infrastructure they control.

deployment_modes.name: Managed cloud
deployment_modes.definition: The vendor operates this system and the user reaches it as a tenant rather than running it.

deployment_modes.name: Optional cloud services
deployment_modes.definition: Adjunct vendor services a self-operated deployment may use without depending on them.

GNU General Public License 3.0 or later
GNU General Public License 2.0 or later

source_models.name: Open source
source_models.definition: Operational code is released under one OSI-approved license.

source_models.name: Mixed open licenses
source_models.definition: Operational code or repository content uses multiple open code or content licenses without production restrictions.

source_models.name: Mixed open and proprietary
source_models.definition: The operational product combines reusable open-source components with a proprietary or restricted core, runtime, or distribution boundary.

source_models.name: Open core
source_models.definition: An open-source core is accompanied by restricted components or enterprise features.

source_models.name: Source available
source_models.definition: Operational source is visible but use, modification, or production deployment is restricted.

source_models.name: Proprietary
source_models.definition: Operational implementation is not provided under reusable source terms.

source_models.name: Unclear
source_models.definition: Available evidence does not yet support a confident source-model conclusion.

dimensions.definition: Direct usefulness as a personal or agentic second brain.
Local-first behavior, exportability, privacy, and user control.
Open formats, APIs, adapters, and model/provider portability.
Retrieval, temporal handling, provenance, consolidation, and contradiction management.
Setup and maintenance burden for a technically capable individual.
Adoption, maintenance, documentation, and production readiness.
Consistency and correctness on the tasks the system claims to handle.
Breadth, quality, and composability of tool invocation.
Ability to plan and complete meaningful multi-step work.
Approvals, steering, boundaries, inspectability, and safe interruption.
Tracing, checkpoints, error visibility, replay, and recovery.
Local execution, privacy, exportability, and operator control.
Provider, tool, protocol, and deployment portability.
Adoption, maintenance, documentation, and production readiness.
Usefulness and consistency across the assistant's documented jobs rather than transient model benchmarks.
Conversation state, project or workspace context, memory controls, and provenance.
Files, search, connectors, applications, and actions available through the product.
Consent, approvals, source visibility, correction, memory controls, and safe interruption.
Retention, training controls, tenant boundaries, administration, privacy, and export or deletion controls.
Model choice, data portability, APIs, protocols, and connector openness.
Platform availability, accessibility, onboarding, and interaction quality.
Stability, support, documentation, adoption, and operational readiness.
